headline: Captree dock talk: blues are stupid, bass went to bed, and everybody's asking the wrong question
subhead: The peanut bunker blitz we called last week is still running the beach — but if you want stripers, you're fishing in the dark now.
body_markdown:
Guy pulls up to the fuel dock yesterday morning, cooler full of ice, no bait, and asks me straight up: "Where are the bass?" I told him what I've been telling everybody all week — you're not going to find them where you found them in June. He looked at me like I'd told him Santa wasn't real.

Here's the truth of it. The water's warm — buoy readings off the beach are sitting around 71, 72 degrees, and that's pushed the stripers clean out of their comfort zone. Bass like it closer to 68-70. When the ocean runs hot like this, those fish don't leave, they just go down and go nocturnal. I'm talking Fire Island Inlet structure, the rockpile off Democrat Point, the deeper cuts along the barrier beach — all producing, but only in that window from last light through the dark hours, and best right around the tide change. Eels and bunker chunks fished tight to structure on the last of the outgoing has been my go-to. Daytime, forget it — you're wasting bait.

Now the bluefish — that's a different conversation entirely, and it's the one I actually want to have with you. We flagged this exact pattern last week, said the blitz would keep running as long as the bunker stayed on the beach and the weather held stable, and here we are — it's still going. Peanut bunker schools are getting pushed right up against the sand from about Cedar Beach down through Kismet and Corneille Estates, and the blues are hammering them in that classic surface-boil, birds-diving, water-turning-white way that makes your heart rate jump even after twenty years of seeing it. I had a customer's kid catch eight blues in twenty minutes off the beach two mornings ago on nothing fancy — a 3/4-ounce Kastmaster in chrome, long cast, fast retrieve right through the froth. Poppers work too if you want the visual, and honestly there's nothing better than watching a blue crash a topwater at first light with the sun coming up over the inlet.

The bigger blues have been mixing in more since around the 27th — not just the schoolies anymore, some real choppers in that 8-10 pound class showing up in the mix. If you're throwing bucktails for bass and getting bit off, that's your answer — it's blues, and they don't care what you had planned.

Fluke's been the steady hand all month, and it still is. Nothing explosive, but dependable, which honestly is what fluke fishing should be. Robert Moses bridges — both spans — are holding fish in that 25 to 35 foot range on the drift, and the pattern hasn't changed: chartreuse bucktail with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer, dragged slow along the bottom, working the current seams where the pilings break the flow. Best window is the last two hours of the outgoing into the start of the incoming, when the bait gets funneled through and the fluke stack up to intercept it. I'm seeing a mix of shorts and keepers, maybe one keeper for every four or five fish in the box — nothing to write home about, but enough to keep rods bent and put dinner on the table if you're patient and keep moving. The channel edges off Captree and out toward the inlet mouth have been holding fish too, especially on that harder-bottom transition where the sand gives way to shell.

Weakfish are around in the bay but it's spotty — a few nice fish coming out of Great South Bay on bucktails and soft plastics fished slow near the bottom, mostly in that deeper water off Sayville and out toward the Fire Island lighthouse flats. Nothing to build a trip around, but worth a drift or two if you're already out there for fluke. Blackfish season's closed right now so we're not chasing tog — that conversation picks back up in the fall.

Tide-wise, we're coming off that full moon push, so the current's still running hard, and we're easing toward neap over the next several days. That's actually good news for the bay bite — less current means the fluke drifts slow down to a manageable pace instead of you having to add extra weight just to feel bottom. Wind's been out of the southwest and stable, which is exactly the kind of pattern that keeps a beach blitz alive — no wind chop pushing the bait off the sand, no dirty water rolling in.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the blues to keep running the beach as long as this weather holds — and this time of year, that's usually until a thunderstorm or a cold front rolls through and scatters everything for a day or two before it resets. Early August tends to bring one of those disruptions, so if you've got a window this week, take it. For bass, I'd keep the program the same — dark hours, structure, patience — and don't be surprised if the first albie or bonito scout reports start trickling in from further east as we push toward the next new moon. That's usually the tell that the season's starting to turn, even if the calendar still says summer down here at Captree.
